Hindmost means furthest to the back — the one positioned at the very rear of a group, line, or series, behind everyone or everything else.

Think of a line of people queuing outside a shop. The very last person standing at the tail end of that line — the one with the most people in front of them — is the hindmost person.

It answers the question: "Who or what is the most behind?"

The word "hind" on its own already means "at the back" or "rear" — you may have heard it in phrases like "hind legs" (the back legs of an animal). "Hindmost" takes that idea and pushes it to its furthest extreme: not just at the back, but the furthest back of all.

It works just like other superlatives:

  • Small → smallest (the most small)
  • Far → farthest (the most far)
  • Hind → hindmost (the most toward the back)

So "hindmost" always implies a comparison. You can only call something hindmost when there are others ahead of it. It is the last of a group, the tail end, the very bottom of a sequence.

Physical position:

  • The hindmost soldier in the march was struggling to keep up.
    (The soldier at the very back, behind all the others.)
  • She chose the hindmost seat in the cinema so no one would sit behind her.
    (The seat furthest to the rear of the hall.)
  • The hindmost carriage of the train was the quietest.
    (The last carriage, at the tail of the train.)

Abstract / figurative use:

  • Safety was the hindmost thought in his reckless mind.
    (Safety was the very last thing he was thinking about — pushed furthest to the back of his concerns.)
  • The new recruits found themselves hindmost in priority when resources were handed out.
    (They were given the least attention, treated as the last in importance.)
An Important Nuance: Position vs. Sequence

"Hindmost" can describe either physical position (who or what is at the back in space) or order/priority (who or what comes last in importance, time, or rank).

Both uses share the same core idea: pushed to the furthest extreme of "behind."
The Famous Phrase: "Devil Take the Hindmost"

This is a well-known expression in English that directly uses this word, and understanding it will cement the meaning for you.

"Devil take the hindmost" means: every person should look after themselves, and whoever is the slowest or the last will suffer the consequences.

It paints the picture of people fleeing in panic. Everyone rushes ahead to save themselves. The devil, chasing from behind, will catch whoever is last — the hindmost person. The message is blunt: don't be last, or you'll pay the price.

This phrase is used today to describe ruthlessly competitive or self-serving behaviour, where nobody helps those who fall behind.
Register and Tone: When Is This Word Used?

"Hindmost" is a formal and somewhat literary word. In everyday conversation, most people would simply say "last," "at the back," or "rearmost." You are more likely to encounter "hindmost" in:

  • Formal writing
  • Literature, especially older texts
  • Fixed expressions like "devil take the hindmost"
  • Military or ceremonial descriptions

It carries a slightly old-fashioned, dignified feel. Using it in casual speech would sound unusually elevated — not wrong, but noticeable.
How It Differs from Similar Words

ConceptWordShade of meaning
  • Last — the most general, everyday word. Can mean last in time, order, or position.
  • Rearmost — very close to "hindmost"; means furthest to the rear. Slightly more technical or spatial.
  • Hindmost — specifically emphasises being furthest behind in a group, with a slightly formal, literary tone. Works for both space and priority.

The distinction is subtle. In most situations, "hindmost" and "rearmost" are interchangeable. The difference is mainly in feel: "rearmost" sounds clinical, while "hindmost" sounds more classical.
Quick Summary to Lock It In

Hindmost = the one that is furthest behind of all — the last, the rearmost, whether in a physical line, a sequence, or a list of priorities. It is a formal, somewhat old-fashioned adjective most famously used in the phrase "devil take the hindmost," which warns that those who fall behind face the worst consequences.
